# Zonorah, Media Neuroscience Lab

> Zonorah is a Media Neuroscience Lab. It writes down what radio, TV and YouTube broadcast and counts it. Open data and studies on commission.

Last updated: 2026-11-24

Zonorah records radio, TV and YouTube, transcribes the audio, and counts how many minutes each topic is on air, on which station and at what time. The audio is deleted after transcription.

Questions the data can answer

## Home

https://zonorah.com/

Zonorah is a Media Neuroscience Lab. It records and counts what media broadcast. Research on the brain is done separately and uses these counts.

## How the numbers are made

1. Record. Each station's live signal comes in over the internet. We record it during the hours of its schedule.
2. Transcribe. A speech-recognition program on our own computer turns the audio into text, with a time for every sentence. Then the audio is deleted.
3. Code. The text is searched for the words each study uses, including their variants. Every passage that matches is entered on a fixed form: who speaks, the role of the person or cause, topic, tone, framing, and whether the claim has evidence or is rumour.
4. Report. The public numbers are minutes on air per 100 hours recorded. Work done on commission arrives as a PDF by email, on the schedule you choose.

## Method

https://zonorah.com/method/

These limits apply to every published figure.

### Limit 1: Transcription errors

The speech-recognition program mishears names, acronyms and brands. A misheard word is not counted, so figures tend to be low.

Try several spellings of the same name

### Limit 2: Recorded hours only

A station that was not recorded at some hour tells nothing about what it broadcast then. Absence from the recording does not mean it was not said.

The coverage table shows what is recorded

### Limit 3: Music and advertising

Recorded minutes include songs and adverts. A word inside an advert is counted.

### Limit 4: Comparing stations

A music station and a news station cannot be compared directly. Compare stations of the same type, or the same word over time.

### Limit 5: Rounding and hidden figures

Public figures are rounded to multiples of 5 and hidden below 3 minutes. With exact low figures, someone could tell whether a named person was mentioned at a given moment. Totals may not add up exactly.

### Citing: Citing a figure

Cite the permanent link of the comparison and the date it was consulted. Figures change when recordings are added.

Zonorah (2026). Minutes on air per 100 hours recorded. Consulted [date], terms: [terms]. [link to the comparison]

## Research

https://zonorah.com/research/

Two lines of work share the same recordings: open data, and studies carried out on commission.

### Scientific research: Open data

For researchers, teachers and journalists. The comparator, the charts, the CSV files and the El Niño index follow rules that are published and fixed, so anyone can check them. An AI assistant answers from the transcripts and quotes short fragments with their station and time.

Every figure: minutes on air per 100 hours recorded

### Commercial research: Studies on commission

An organisation chooses the sources, keywords and rules. Each mention is entered on a fixed form, including risk and urgency, and a PDF is sent by email on the schedule the organisation chooses. The public data does not show who commissioned what.

Not tied to a country: the client picks the stations and their language. Reports in English, Spanish or Indonesian

### Foundations: Origin of the approach

The Media Neuroscience Lab at UC Santa Barbara works, among other topics, on moral narratives in news and entertainment, text mining and large media datasets. Zonorah uses that computational approach. It does no brain imaging and runs no experiments with participants. Research on the brain is done separately and uses these figures.

medianeuroscience.org ↗

## Zonorah Data

https://zonorah.com/data/

How many minutes a word was on air, by station and by day.

### Compare: Comparator

Up to four words at once, grouped by station, day, hour, region or type of station. The search ignores capital letters and accents and includes variants.

The coverage table shows which stations and hours are recorded

### Download: Downloads and charts

Each comparison downloads as a CSV file with the same columns as the table. The same comparison can be embedded in an article as a chart that shows its source.

### Ask: AI assistant

It summarises the transcripts and quotes short fragments with station and time. It does not give names or data of private individuals. Transcripts are automatic, so a summary can contain mistakes.

## Privacy

https://zonorah.com/privacy/

No recordings are kept. This page says what is kept about people who sign in. It is a draft pending legal review.

### Recordings: None are kept

The audio is deleted as soon as it has been turned into text. Only the text stays.

### Your account: What is stored if you sign in with Google

Your email and name as Google gives them, the date you joined and the date of your last visit, how many questions you ask each day, and which sector reports you download.

The password is handled by Google. It is not stored here.

### Your questions: They go to an AI service

A question is sent to an AI service (Groq, in the United States) without your email or name. The text of your questions is not kept with your account. Please do not write personal data in a question.

### How long: Until you delete the account

A session lasts 30 days. Your data stays while the account exists. You can delete the account whenever you want, and everything goes: email, name, sessions and question count.

### Your rights: Access, correction, deletion

You can ask for access to your data, for it to be corrected or for it to be deleted by writing to hola@zonorah.com.

### Status: Draft pending legal review

The wording may change after the review. Companies that order studies are covered by their own agreement, not by this page.

Contact: hola@zonorah.com
